This is achieved in the context of a topological abelian group G, where its topological Borel schema P(G) serves as a Boolean algebra that corresponds to the compact open topology. Leveraging the group's action on itself, which is continuous given certain conditions, we effectively demonstrate Pontryagin duality through the execution of a G-action on the type spectrum Spec(T_G), thereby illustrating Pontryagin duality as a manifestation of Stone duality. Spec(T_G) represents the type spectrum of the reduced product Q_R of the set of non-zero reals equipped with the quotient topology, which is also the Stone space of its Boolean algebra of clopen sets. Consequently, the prime types correspond to the elements of P(G), and continuous type-preserving actions correspond to Pontryagin dually continuous actions, and the type spectrum Spec(T_G) corresponds to the dual space X of G. Moreover, the reduced product Q_R serves as the spatial realization of G. Furthermore, any topological abelian group G, which is in addition to its topological properties also equipped with an action by another group H, which is also topologically active, leads to a corresponding action of the group H on the type spectrum Spec(T_G), which is in accordance with Pontryagin duality. In contrast, while continuous actions of topological abelian groups, which are not necessarily spatial, may possess Pontryagin dually continuous actions, these actions are unencapsulated as actions on the type spectrum Spec(T_G). This method presents a significant improvement by circumventing the necessity of the phase-randomization property of laser sources. Nevertheless, the TF-QKD framework still relies on the synchronization of two distinct optical frequencies, which poses difficulties in terms of implementation. This paper describes a solution to eliminate the synchronization requirement by utilizing a universal quantum source, thereby simplifying the TF-QKD framework. Furthermore, the proposed scheme offers a substantial enhancement in security by combining TF-QKD with the principle of measurement-device independence, thereby providing an unconditional security protection for quantum communication. The experiment demonstrated that the combined scheme achieved a secure key rate of 1.27 bits per quantum bit even over an impressive distance of 482 kilometers. The findings from this research are anticipated to facilitate significant progress in the development of long-distance quantum communication technology. 

As an extension of the proposed scheme, we successfully demonstrated a hierarchical TF-QKD network involving three nodes, and achieved a secure key rate of 1.23 bits per quantum bit over a combined distance of 854 kilometers. The experiment proved that the modular design of the TF-QKD framework results in a considerable improvement in scalability. Consequently, the proposed scheme is deemed suitable for real-world quantum communication applications.

To address this challenge, we focus on building object detectors using limited, annotated data. Recent approaches have utilized existing, unlabeled data to improve the quality of annotated objects, but we propose an alternative method where the unlabeled data represents the object categories directly, eliminating the need for additional processing. Leveraging pre-trained feature extractors, we train an object detector on unlabeled data, then combine the results with the annotated data to create the final detection output. This novel approach, which utilizes a self-supervised model to represent object categories, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the COCO and OpenImages datasets. On the COCO dataset, our method achieves a masked AP of 24.4 with just 500 annotated images, outperforming models without category information and other contrastive methods. Furthermore, our method exhibits exceptional performance on datasets with a high number of object categories, achieving a masked AP of 16.8 on the OpenImages dataset with only 30 annotated images. This is a notable improvement of 11.1% over the traditional bounding box detection method. Videos accompanying this paper can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/freecatd/. The implementation of our method is based on the anchor-based bounding box detector, but we are exploring the adaptation of other detection paradigms as future work. In our investigation, we gather human ratings on the quality of professionally translated texts through a crowdsourcing platform and employ these ratings to analyze TQA's consistency, as well as to recover underlying quality metrics believed to underlie human translation assessments. Ultimately, our investigation raises questions about employing agreement analysis to assess human assessors, as well as the reliability of employing these quality metrics to train objective evaluation metrics due to their low consistency.  We aim to explore TQA's reliability from a new perspective, providing valuable insights for researchers working in automatic evaluation of translation quality.  As far as our knowledge goes, this study represents the initial investigation aiming to quantify TQA's reliability.  Our findings also provide initial insights into human rating variability, as well as the potential challenges of obtaining reliable translation quality metrics from human assessors. interactive graph search groups specific labels in a structured framework and presents them on a interface, requiring users to identify target items while learning from provided information and constraints. Although optimization problems have been the focus of recent research, addressing query efficiency in these situations has been largely overlooked. This paper examines the feasibility of searching large graphs interactively by comparing the space requirements of graph- and item-based query representations. Our analysis of existing graph decomposition techniques sheds light on the importance of a graph's structure in predicting query patterns. Moreover, we introduce a new method called BiT-Top, which uses binary search on the labels at the bottom of a graph's tree structure to estimate the quantity of desired items and determine an optimal search path. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world graphs, including Twitter data and the Yale university's faculty website, demonstrate the diversity of search patterns observed across different graph types, highlighting the need for a personalized approach to query optimization. Our results also showcase the effectiveness of BiT-Top in reducing overall search space by an average of 47.1%, particularly when dealing with thousands of items on a graph. Finally, our analysis of graph properties has helped us identify potential graph characteristics that could lead to predictable query patterns, paving the way for a personalized query optimization framework. This discovery is the first step towards a signature-based approach to optimize interactive graph search, which we will explore further in future research. Empirical models, although computationally simple, are often inaccurate due to oversimplifications in their statistical basis. In contrast, deterministic models, like those based on ray tracing and computational methods, require significant resources and cannot be applied in real-time due to the time-consuming process of creating the initial terrain database. This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. This phenomenon, which has been closely observed and measured, is entirely attributable to the impact of the sound waves on the gel's microstructure, where particles become rearranged and suspended in a process known as "Lindemann instability." What's more, the exact moment at which the gels transition from solid to liquid under sonic force has been precisely pinpointed, marking the first time this specific capability has been documented in gels. Our study, which was conducted using gels made from a mixture of polyacrylamide and water, opens the door for further exploration of the many practical applications of this innovative discovery. We propose that ultrasonic waves could potentially be utilized as a low-cost method for creating and handling gel-based materials, much like the conventional use of mixers and stirrers. Our findings also hold significant potential for the creation of targeted drug delivery systems, specifically those utilizing gels as the delivery method. We further suggest that ultrasonic waves could potentially be used to eliminate clogs in gel-based materials, much like the use of ultrasound for medical purposes. Lastly, our study highlights the significant similarity between the acoustic properties observed in biological tissues and those observed in the rheo-acoustic gels used in the study, potentially opening the door for the use of ultrasonic waves as a diagnostic and treatment method. This study presents an in-depth numerical analysis that accurately models heat transfer within the fluid and its impact on laser interaction. The study examines and explains the occurrence of negative propagation coefficients, backscattered beams, and beam splitting effects resulting from laser propagation. The investigation focuses on laser pulse duration variations, ranging from a few nanoseconds to millisecond durations, and their effects on laser propagation, absorption, and production of plasma within the fluid. The results reveal that for short laser pulses, the generated plasma has a very high absorption coefficient, leading to increased laser absorption. Conversely, for longer laser pulses, the presence of plasma induces significant negative propagation coefficients and backscattered beams, while reduced plasma formation results in decreased laser absorption. The outcomes of this study demonstrate the significance of numerical modeling in understanding laser propagation and its interaction with the surrounding fluid, particularly for laser pulse duration variations. The findings also emphasize the limitation of simplified analytical models in accurately predicting laser behavior within the fluid. Ultimately, the study suggests that for long laser pulses, the emergence of negative propagation coefficients and backscattered beams cannot be solely attributed to backscattered ripples; rather, the effect stems from a complex interplay of diffuse scattering within the fluid, particularly within the laminar-to-turbulent transition zone near the laser beam axis. Furthermore, the study suggests that diffuse scattering accounts for nearly all the unwanted effects previously reported in the literature as 'negative propagation coefficients, backscattered beams, and beam splitting effects.' It is expected that the study's comprehensive results will facilitate further research on laser propagation within the fluid. This study examines the accuracy of ATLAS and CMS in distinguishing between Top and Bottom mixing with Standard Model-like particles and Standard Model particles mixing with non-Standard Model-like particles at the LHC. We consider a scenario where a particle (phion) decays into a top quark and a pair of jets and utilize a multi step strategy to discover this phenomenon, initially representing the phion as a broad resonance and applying a maximum likelihood (ML) fit to locate the signal. This procedure was applied to a simulated ATLAS dataset from 13 TeV, consisting of 37.5 fb^-1 of luminosity, as well as a simulated CMS dataset from 13 TeV, consisting of 139 fb^-1 of luminosity, in search of the signal: tph, hpht, Bottom-phion signals: Bph, Hpt and a background of Top colour neutral coupled Standard Model like particles : tc, tc5. This work highlights the feasibility of directly discovering Top and Bottom companions at the LHC by inferring the presence of these particles through their subsequent decays into well known Top and Bottom systems. However, NeRFs face significant challenges when using structured optimization to generate high-quality images due to its slow convergence.  To address this issue, we introduce a new technique called puff, which significantly simplifies the input data and uses a structured noise model to improve convergence during optimization. Experimentally, puff far surpasses the current state-of-the-art 3D scene generation methods, achieving even higher accuracy on the benchmark benchmark and smooth video rendering. To facilitate future research into structured 3D scene generation, we introduce a new benchmark and dataset called benchmark.surf and make the puff code and 3D scene generation benchmark available for public use. Recent advances in deep learning have transformed wildfire detection, but the task remains a significant challenge due to the intricate dynamics of fire propagation. Traditional methods rely on threshold-based analysis of time-series satellite data to identify this complex phenomenon, but the subtlety of fire patterns often leads to undetected incidents and false alarms. In an effort to address these limitations, a new deep learning model, Temp-WDNet, is introduced for improved preemptive wildfire detection. Temp-WDNet is a dynamic network that automatically learns to recognize the distinctive temporal patterns of fire evolution from multi-spectral time-series data. Temp-WDNet detects active fires by mapping the data sequences of a region of interest to a one-dimensional distribution function. In the second stage, the model identifies individual fire sources by analyzing data sequences separated by natural breaks in the distribution. Temp-WDNet is evaluated using two extensive fire datasets from different regions and is compared to several benchmark methods. Experimental results demonstrate the model's superior detection performance, along with the substantial undetection reduction and false alarm rate decrease it achieves. In particular, the model is found to outperform existing approaches by up to 10% in terms of overall detection accuracy. In addition, the Temp-WDNet source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/andreashawyield/Temp-WDNet. This initiative aims to establish a collaborative research community for improving wildfire detection using advanced deep learning methods. We welcome researchers, engineers, and practitioners to contribute to the development of new techniques and participate in the advancement of this critical area. Furthermore, the implementation of Temp-WDNet on Google Earth Engine enables seamless integration of the model into existing wildfire detection workflows, facilitating undetected fire detection and improved accuracy in emergency response systems. In a second study, we introduce an innovative deep learning method, FireNet2, for accurately mapping fire extent from fire radiative energy data. FireNet2 leverages a Semi-Supervised Machine Learning framework, in which it uses initial fire detection information and geometric properties of firefootprints to initialize a model for predicting fire spatial extent. FireNet2 is evaluated using fire radiative energy data from the 2006 FireMapbox dataset and is compared to several Benchmark Methods. Experimental results demonstrate the substantial improvement in accuracy and reduction in undetected fire areas compared to the benchmark methods. In particular, the model is found to outperform existing approaches by up to 20% in terms of overall accuracy. This work is publicly accessible at: https

Observing social media expression patterns is highly advantageous for identifying mental health, since individuals tend to convey their emotions openly on these platforms.  While current systems utilize social media data to diagnose mental health, accurately gauging depression levels is vital for informed treatment decisions. a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges. 
We reveal that the order processing mechanism results in token value diminishment for market liquidity suppliers under circumstances of heightened token price volatility. 
AMMs are adopted predominantly when their supported token combinations have significant utility and market demand. 
However, the steeper price curves (greater token value increment with increased token quantity) of AMMs facilitate arbitrage, resulting in suppressed market liquidity. 
Yet, supplementary products (token pairs) can boost overall market liquidity, although this is countered by the risk of collapse associated with those products. 
A statistical model is used to evaluate the likelihood of failure for each token, taking into account the number of products offering market exposure to that token. 
The results show that a negative relationship exists between the number of supporting products and the token's collateral value. 
This is specifically observed in the case of smaller markets, while an opposite effect is seen in markets characterized by intense competition and high transaction volumes, 
where a larger number of supporting products is associated with enhanced market liquidity and decreased failure risk, perhaps due to the diversification effect provided by a large market product portfolio. 
This empirical research is complementary to existing theoretical AMM models, thereby broadening our collective understanding of the mechanisms underpinning these decentralized exchanges. 
Finally, our study is cross-checked against another major AMM platform, Binance Spot, yielding comparable outcomes. 
The research is further supported by case studies featuring the cryptocurrency market. 
The experiments show that AMMs utilizing a larger portfolio of supporting products are more likely to withstand failure, particularly during times of market downturn. 
This illustrates the synergistic effect of market stability and potential future applications in cryptocurrency markets. 
The research is further complemented by qualitative interviews conducted with three market participants, 
who confirm that the platform's token diversity plays a significant role in diminishing the risk of failure, especially during periods of market downturn. 
The research is further evaluated through an experiment using real-world data to test the relationship between the token failure probability and the number of supporting products,

Various cryogenic platforms already exist, but their complexity and custom nature make them less suitable as a common global benchmark. Our model, founded on established RF technologies, is a more practical alternative, and this paper details its potential and limitations. 
This work at Fermilab's Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center is the initial phase of a research project focused on developing a universal cryogenic platform for future use in commercial quantum computing applications. 
This paper explores the potential for commercial use of such a platform and compares it to current, more customized solutions. Our study identifies key advantages of the proposed model which enables a more cohesive global community and facilitates widespread collaboration and knowledge sharing. 
At the same time, we recognize the existing platforms's capabilities and the need for further development to reach commercial maturity. This work represents a starting point in the development of a more comprehensive and platform-independent approach to cryogenic solutions for quantum computing. 
These novel approaches in the field of cryogenic and quantum computing hold the potential to simplify the design and implementation of large-scale quantum computers and facilitate a more open and collaborative global community and industry. 
This work is supported by the National Quantum Initiative and the Department of Energy's research at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab.

annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts lack standardized sentence structures and orthographies, making automated POS tagging more complex and error-prone. In light of these complexities, instead of assigning single tags with uncertainty, POS tagging algorithms should allow for probabilistic outcomes. We propose applying the concept of set-valued prediction, enabling POS taggers to suggest a set of potential tags rather than guessing a single one. The objective is to strike a balance between ensuring a high percentage of correct tags while minimizing false positives. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating set-valued prediction into existing state-of-the-art POS tagging algorithms yields more accurate and realistic output, especially when dealing with unknown words. The proposed approach is examined on a variety of historical corpora, including the Huckleberry Finn, Serbian novels from the 19th century (Domaci and Strani), and Greek newspapers from the early 20th century (To Vradyneio and Acropolis). Furthermore, a web-based tool is provided for facilitating hands-on interactions with the set-valued POS tagger. The tool can be accessed via this link: https://set-valued-positagging.github.io/index.html. The set-valued approach has also been utilized to develop a semantic search filter for discovering relevant historical passages. A corresponding demonstration can be found here: https://set-valued-positagging.github.io/search-filter.html. The proposed methodology offers several benefits, including the discovery of unknown words or proper nouns with tag suggestions from the model, the visualization of tags assigned to words in a selected passage, and the option to switch the model's behavior to prefer correctness over unknown tags. Additionally, set-valued tagging enables the automatic detection of words with anomalous tag profiles by comparing the suggested tags with a corpus's tag-clouds. The developed approach has the potential to enhance known-item detection, a pivotal task in digital forensics and information retrieval, by identifying unusual words in historical texts. The method involves computing a similarity metric (such as Jaccard's index) between the suggested tags of a detected item and a known proper noun. If their tags have a high degree of overlap, the suggestion is considered a strong cue. Experimental results show that this approach yields a 23.9% recall score. By incorporating error reversal into the circuit evolution, we find that the gradient calculation can be shifted to a lower error regime, thus scaling more efficiently with the number of qubits. This strategy is demonstrated through a simplified implementation of the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), where the optimal cost function is determined after a single iteration of inverse rotation. Although this approach incurs additional overhead, it significantly boosts the algorithm's performance by leveraging a smaller trial wavefunction for subsequent iterations. To validate this method, we run two quantum simulations, one for a two-qubit quantum system and another for a four-qubit Jordan-Wigner model, comparing the VQE accuracy and convergence time with the conventional strategy. The results show that the hidden inverse method yields a substantial improvement in computational complexity, up to two times more efficient than the conventional approach, given a sufficient number of qubits. This strategy presents a valuable solution for quantum computing on the emerging large-scale quantum hardware near prototype stage. In the category of sets, the best partial order approximation of the image in such a case is obtained by applying the Sierpinski epimorphism followed by the surjection. In categories that are not set-based, the Sierpinski epimorphism may not be available. This paper introduces a concept, called conservative extensions, that can serve a similar purpose in categories that are bounded by equations, providing a way to preserve the order structure in categories where the Sierpinski epimorphism is not available. It demonstrates the existence of such conservative extensions in representable, element-based, and finitely present categories, including certain finite category constructions. Additionally, the paper introduces the notion of quasi-orders and demonstrates the existence of such extensions in categories of quasi-orders as well. In finite category constructions, the paper shows that the Sierpinski epimorphism can be replaced with a different morphism, called the Skula epimorphism, and investigates relationships between this morphism and conservative extensions, highlighting their similarity and the condition for equality. Conservative extensions are also found to be meaningful in the context of infinite infinite-complement properties, and the paper proves that any infinite-complement extension of the finite category $\mathbb T_1$ can be viewed as a conservative extension of the Skula epimorphism. Finally, the paper introduces the concept of upper-adaptive extensions as a subclass of conservative extensions and proves that these extensions exist naturally in several finite category constructions, including copowerings, wrenerings, semirectangles, and finite line graphs. Informally, the upper-adaptive extension represents the minimal partial order approximation in these category constructions. The paper concludes by indicating the potential application of another subclass of conservative extensions, known as lower-adaptive extensions, to investigate certain properties of below-universal categories. This involves proving that above-universal categories are naturally lower-adaptive extensions of the Skula epimorphism. A notable outcome of this investigation is the discovery that a natural number is existent in an infinite-complement, below-universal category if and only if it exists in the finite category $\mathbb T_1$ or its image under a conservative extension of the Skula epimorphism. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers. pathology and radiology is undergoing significant transformation.  Despite research-based promising outcomes with ML models, there is an underlying barrier to integrating these into clinical practices due to issues of interoperability.  The DICOM standard provides specifications for the representation, storage, and exchange of digital images and related information but the standard's complexity poses an obstacle to adoption in the ML field.  Therefore, there is a need for simplified data processing software and tools to facilitate the use of DICOM standard in ML context.  This paper provides an overview of ML and DICOM, discussing existing challenges and presenting novel approaches to resolve them using software called Dictatus.  The Dictatus tool is introduced, which translates DICOM files into a readable tensor form for ML use, and the feasibility of using Dictatus with hybrid, distributed, and batch processing is demonstrated through 3D image processing applications.  The usual ML pipeline is explained through Dictatus, involving data augmentation, training, evaluation, and prediction, with implementation examples based on CT, MRI, and digital pathology scans. 
Furthermore, the interconnection between Dictatus and other key technologies, such as software containers and automated ML learning pipelines, is illustrated and demonstrated through Dictatus's integration with the CWF and LIFEScience workflows.  Lastly, the potential future development for Dictatus is explored, particularly in terms of extending the ML pipeline to cover data annotation, enrichment and automatic classification, as well as integrating Dictatus with the emerging Clinical Pathological Analysis (CPA) standards.  The long-term aim is to promote CPA as a standard in biosciences and medicine through the NCI's CPA initiative.  It is anticipated that CPA will facilitate the classification of cellular and tissue pathological conditions and will enable the representation of distinct disease types which can then be modelled using ML techniques.  The classical ML approach typically relies on supervised learning with homogeneous data sets which limits the representation of complex diseases that usually have varied clinical features and individual effective treatments.  The integration of CPA standard will enable the representation of various clinical conditions which can then be exchanged and processed through the DICOM standard in the ML field.  The feasibility of using CPA is currently tested through a pilot project at the National Center for Cancer and Tumor Diseases in Berlin, Germany.  The CPA pilot project is used to build a hierarchical classification model which classifies the unique clinical conditions and treatments based on the primary medical expertise of the treating doctor.  The classification model is built using ML learning pipeline with data from the CPA initiative and the clinical data is provided

A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines conventional longitudinal and transverse scans to mimic human operation, showing promising results in measuring blood vessel depth and identifying potential issues like scoliosis deformity and rib prominence. This study assessed whether the robotic scanner can accurately replicate longitudinal and transverse scans, as well as compensate for operator variability. Ten experienced radiologists performed both conventional and robotic scans of 25 healthy volunteers, and the findings showed the robotic scanner effectively mimicked both longitudinal and transverse scans, and helped reduce variability caused by different operators. Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.  Further, the paper establishes that these new powerdomains naturally arise in denotational semantics of non-deterministic programming languages with a high level of concurrency.  It also introduces a topology on directed spaces known as the convex topology and proves an equivalence between this topology's compact sets and the convex powerdomain's objects.  Moreover, the paper introduces and investigates the convex convex-powerdomain and a natural interpretation of the partial map functor, showing how these concepts align with non-deterministic concurrent programming.  Finally, the paper explores relationships between fine powerspaces of directed spaces and the finiteness semantics of concurrent programs, proposing a further extension to the fine convex powerdomain and its relationship to a partial commutative monoid representing the program's finite behavior.  It also introduces a new notion of convex finiteness and an extended finiteness semantics by considering the convergence of finite collections of values in a directed structure, and both the convex and fine powerspaces have similar structures in this framework.  A significant observation from this extension is the creation of new structures that fail to be directed-complete but possess the finiteness property, and the original powerdomain structures are shown to be substructures within this extended concept.  As a result, the notion of partial map categories indexed by a directed structure fails to have an adequate partial commutative monoid, and a possible future extension to the fine convex powerdomain and semantics is discussed. In contrast to typical cooling effects, 'hothouse' climates are distinguished by a blocked window region for water vapor, which has led to theories about the role of cloud feedback for maintaining or entering such states. In contrast to these theories, our research reveals that clear skies are the primary driver of the 'hothouse' low atmospheric heating by blocking water vapor transmission. Utilizing the idealized 'dry hothouse' experiment and the 'Dry Hothouse' experiment with the 'Interactive Cloud Model,' we have exposed the clear-sky water vapor 'window effect,' which occurs when water vapor transmission is blocked by the spectrum at the top of the atmosphere, resulting in the 'hothouse' low atmospheric heating. Furthermore, the study found that 'hothouse' clouds act as an amplifier by enhancing the effects of clear-sky water vapor by blocking water vapor transmission. 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task on extracting text from a specific region, supported by a provided mask if the text was partially obscured.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity in recognition accuracy between previously seen and novel text, with an average of 67.32% demonstrated by all participants' submissions across the test set.
The scenario highlighted a considerable gap in current OCR technology regarding adapting to new, unseen words and emphasized the need for further research in this area to achieve higher practical real-world application effectiveness. Future work is also suggested on enhancing the methodology for creating representative test sets for OOV detection and extraction. Potential areas for exploration include involving broader communities in the development of OCR technology and incorporating the utilization of Web-based crowdsourcing platforms to gather a more diverse and representative dataset for OOV detection and extraction. Furthermore, future research can also focus on reducing the noticeable discrepancy in recognition accuracy between previously seen and novel text. Lastly, supplementary videos can be accessed via https://sites.google.com/view/oov-challenge-2022, showcasing the performance of top-three participants' submissions. The challenge was successfully implemented through the collaborative efforts of the IAPC community, supported by the Alibaba Group, and complemented by the resources from CRCHudson and the MoE R&D Challenges. current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian unfolding approach commonly used in high-energy physics experiments in a way that scales effectively with the number of qubits. Our approach achieves this by treating the measurement errors associated with a multi-qubit circuit as a Bayesian model and develops an optimal posterior distribution. To validate this approach, we compare it with standard MEM techniques using experiments involving both real-world circuits and ideal simulations. Our results indicate that the unfolded method yields more accurate probabilities while being highly scalable, even for circuits with a large number of qubits. Furthermore, we examine its applicability to the calculation of expectation values. Unlike probabilities, we found that scaling issues arise when the number of qubits exceeds 10. To address this, we suggested a possible extension of the unfolded approach. Our findings also highlight the difference in scaling limitations between probabilities and expectation values. Our work demonstrates the potential for a more scalable and reliable measurement error correction method, which could lead to a new and improved paradigm for quantum metrology using near-term computers. To facilitate the use of our approach, we provide a Python implementation that includes both real-world and ideal circuit simulation capabilities, integrated with the qiskit IBMQ provider for easy deployment on real quantum computers via the qiskit QEDK framework. Our unfolded measurement error correction code can be accessed via the qedk-measurement-errors repository on GitHub. Our proposal is a new method that correlates qubit readings to derive a probability distribution, treating measurement errors as a Bayesian model. To assess its validity and scalability, we compared it with established methods for several circuits and simulations. Our findings indicate that it yields more accurate results and can handle a greater number of qubits. To facilitate its use, we provide the Python code used to generate these results as part of the qedk project on GitHub. Our new approach is scalable, yet still guarantees the accuracy of the probabilities, which is particularly appealing for its potential to scale up to complex multi-qubit systems. Our findings suggest the unfolded method could be a promising alternative for quantum metrology using near-term computers. Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as machine learning models can assist medical professionals in decision-making to enhance patient care or identify rare medical conditions through pattern recognition. However, most current datasets consist of standardized, anonymized records that lack the richness of real-world variability and real-time data, which often includes incomplete and uncorrected patient information. Therefore, developing and training high-performing machine learning models for real-world applications is essential, but doing so requires access to comprehensive and up-to-date patient information, which often poses significant challenges due to data completeness and accuracy, as well as tight data protection regulations. This study examines the complete and accurate patient information challenge in the context of sequential clinical prediction tasks, such as identifying patients with a higher risk of developing a particular condition through the representation learning approach. While the idea of training models to represent the complete and accurate patient information directly is appealing, it often proves impractical due to the presence of inaccuracies or incomplete data and the continuous evolution of medical knowledge and clinical guidelines. Moreover, the presence of inaccuracies or incomplete data often results in the generation of noisy labels, which pose significant challenges to sequence-based clinical prediction tasks, as evidenced by recent studies demonstrating even the most advanced neural networks can achieve high prediction accuracy despite containing noisy labels. This study examines the noisy label problem in the context of machine learning for clinical data, and investigates how the noisy label distribution impacts model performance across various clinical tasks. Ultimately, the study proposes a method for estimating the reliable patient information even in the presence of noisy labels, and demonstrates how the proposed method can support the representation learning for clinical applications. This study achieves the proposed method using a clinical data reasoning model that mimics the human learning process, and demonstrates the results show that the proposed method is effective when the noisy label distribution varies across different models, and the proposed method is effective when the predicted variable is an intermediate state in a patient treatment sequence. This study demonstrates the proposed method can support the sequence-based clinical prediction learning. Moreover, the proposed method is effective when the noisy label distribution is sampled from the actual clinical data, and the proposed method is effective even when the treatment sequence is unknown. This study demonstrates the proposed method can support the sequential clinical prediction learning. Finally, the proposed method is effective when the patient information is not from actual patients but from populations, and the proposed method is effective when the patient treatment sequence is unknown. This study demonstrates the proposed method supports the population-based clinical prediction learning. This research is conducted using a clinical prediction learning task

, a new type of hybrid network is suggested that blends rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  This hybrid network creates edges according to a mixture of these rules.  Specifically, when a new edge is added, it follows the preferential attachment rule with a certain probability and otherwise forms between two randomly selected nodes.  This approach leads to a distribution of node in- and out-degrees that has less extreme outliers compared to a purely preferential attachment network, thereby improving upon this traditional model.  Inference methods applicable to the new model are then explored and demonstrated with actual network data.  Furthermore, the advantages of this model are illustrated through its ability to establish relationships between nodes not yet connected by preferentially attached edges.  Ultimately, the potential uses and applications of this model in other network analysis contexts are also discussed.  In particular, the model presents an innovative solution for tackling the challenges of network data analysis.  Moreover, the model's ideas can serve as a starting point for further development and exploration in other areas of network analysis research.  In addition to the text and figures in this article, supplementary material including further figures and the network data used in the study are available at: https://github.com/linlinxu/HPA_network. Traditionally, Gaussian Process researchers have either designed kernels from scratch, obtained them from kernels banks, or developed kernel grammars to create combinations of basic kernels. Although prior methods successfully discovered suitable kernels, they often struggled to understand the relative merits of various kernels. Gaussian Process kernels can be represented as matrices or strings generated by graph-based operations, enabling the creation of a Gaussian Process kernel space. By utilizing this characterization, we propose a novel Gaussian Process classifier that identifies the most effective kernel for a specific task by analyzing the kernel space. Our approach is straightforward, allowing it to function with limited computational resources and can be easily integrated into current Gaussian Process workflows. We tested the proposed classifier on real-world data sets, demonstrating its ability to select kernels similar to those preferred by experts as well as outperform traditional methods in several instances. Moreover, our classifier can facilitate the discovery of new kernels by identifying unsampled regions in the kernel space, which we believe presents an exciting area for further investigation. Research has shown that systems aligned with specific symmetry properties can be categorized based on a modified effective dimensionality metric that takes into consideration the roles of coupling constants and field strengths. We extend this concept to a class of systems where the field variables undergo a smooth spatial transformation, resulting in the introduction of novel dimensionality metrics. Furthermore, a theoretical framework allowing for the systematic analysis of systems with the aforementioned characteristics has been developed. This approach, rooted in a modified version of Weyl's formula for fermion systems, yields a refined approximation for the critical temperatures of various models, including the Kondo temperature in the case of fermion-boson systems. Additionally, this method has also helped predict specific characteristics of $\phi^2\psi$ interaction models at zero temperature. The research findings also reveal the existence of a long-sought fermion-boson "trivial" phase in nature, allowing for the successful explanation of the experimentally observed suppression of superconductivity in YBa$_2$Cu$_{3-x}$O$_{6\,x}$ materials. Similar phase shifts have also been predicted for other materials, including La$_2$CuO$_4$, YBa$_2$CuO$_4$, YBa$_2$CuO$_{4+x}$ and YBa$_2$Cu$_{3-x}$O$_{6\,x}$. A significant reason for this is that tests are created by individual programmers rather than by a team of experts specifically designed to write tests, namely, programming and testing professionals. These specialized professionals, known as software testers, are skilled in identifying and critiquing software issues, yet their expertise is often underutilized when writing unit tests by developers, who struggle with testing complex code parts and conflate testing code components with creating unit tests. Through an in-depth data-driven investigation, we investigated, among other things, how software developers interact with testing professionals, code unit testing tools, and test management interface software applications. Our study revealed four distinct patterns of developer behavior: 1) working in a testing environment; 2) writing tests away from the testing environment; 3) writing tests using the testing environment but not directly creating unit tests; and 4) writing unit tests outside the testing environment but still creating unit tests. A closer examination of these patterns highlighted experts' utilization of specialized tools and interface software applications, yet developers infrequently take advantage of these resources to create high-quality unit tests. These findings emphasize the need for developers to collaborate with experts in an integrated environment, where experts will handle tasks outside their expertise, allowing developers to fully engage in writing unit tests with optimal quality. Furthermore, our study underlined developers' challenges with testing code parts and the importance of experts' expertise in identifying issues and providing feedback, as well as improving development experience. These observations prompted us to propose a new model of integrated developer and testing professional cooperation, where experts in an environment link to developers' environment to create unit tests together, leading to increased quality. Our proposed model was validated by testing professionals who shared their expertise and experience in a series of in-depth interviews, where we learned about experts' and developers' overlapping workflows in real-world projects, as well as developers' desire for experts to create unit tests together. Our study finally revealed four key areas for future investigation: 1) how to ensure consistency between developer code and testing code; 2) developing a transition strategy for existing unit tests; 3) creating a strategy for and training developers in creating complex system and integration tests; and 4) developing advice for coding best practices to ensure created unit tests are also good code. These proposed areas for investigation were based on experts' and developers' discussion of future challenges, as well as developers' desire for experts to create system and integration tests. Consequently, we recommend utilizing depth and segmentation maps for eye-in-hand camera calibration rather than directly predicting the camera's position from the image or using PnP calculations based on keypoints. Most network measures were initially developed for simple undirected networks.
As a result, weighted network extensions were created to incorporate weight-based information, particularly for calculating the local clustering coefficient.
We discovered that not all these extensions consider the weights fully; some depend on the degree and react sensitively to even small weight changes, a limitation we call "hybrid."
For our research, we focused on a group of undirected networks where the direction of edges doesn't matter and developed a set of weighted network measures that consider the weights fully, therefore effectively measuring the structure a weighted network presents without being affected by spurious details. 
We demonstrated the efficacy of our new measures by applying them to artificial and real-life scenarios where weighted network structures were evident but the traditional measures failed to reveal.
Using our new measures, we found that the clustering in these scenarios was often caused by a degree-related characteristic rather than the actual weighted structure.
We also found that our newly designed local clustering measures are computationally efficient and can be used for similar edge-based network analyses.
All our implementations are now publicly available as part of the R package NetInfo.

These models have been observed to perform well with smaller training datasets, excel in generalizing outcomes, and reduce training time. This paper demonstrates the advantages of using PINNs compared to purely data-driven neural networks in terms of both training performance and gaining insights into the quality of the approximated solutions. By considering PINNs that are trained with an underlying ordinary differential equation, we derive a strict upper limit on their prediction error, applicable even for data not included in the training phase and without prior knowledge of the true solution. As a crucial step in verifying PINNs, this error estimation process provides assurance on their reliability. To exemplify the practical application of our results, we test the error estimator on two theoretical test problems, including one that showcases the potential for model-predictive control. Finally, a theoretical assessment is carried out to clarify the relationship between the error estimator and the classical error estimate found in the literature for collocation methods. Building on this analysis, a two-step approach is proposed to enhance the PINNs method, combining residual-based equations with a constraint satisfaction technique, ultimately leading to strictly satisfying the original equations. This step is demonstrated to have a crucial impact on the performance of the error estimator. Numerical experiments reveal that the proposed integrated method boasts improved error estimation results compared to using PINNs alone. Moreover, the results indicate that incorporating constraints in the optimizations problem is necessary to guarantee the satisfaction of the underlying equations. This theoretical method is the first attempt at combining the classical methods of constraint satisfaction with machine learning techniques, a integration that is discussed in this study. It is worth noting that the theoretical calculations conducted in this research are quite involved and require a deep understanding of both neural networks and the error estimation techniques. Although the methods are closely related, there has not been any previous attempt to connect them. This research is the first to its knowledge that links these two areas by means of a strict error estimator. A separate computational study is conducted to assess the effectiveness of the theoretical models against some specialized test problems. To enrich the insights into the quality of the approximated solutions, a quantitative measure of the error involving the exact solution of the underlying equation is employed in this study. These experiments include the evaluation of the theoretical error estimate, the construction of the prior model and its subsequent estimation of the total error, the evaluation of the error estimator, and the evaluation of the satisfaction of the equations by the prior model. In specific cases where the action space has a constant Hessian and the expected regret is sub-linear in the number of steps, we show that the minimum eigenvalue grows with $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ for large $n$. Notably, this lower bound surpasses the known achievement of Classical Linear Bandit algorithms, which have achieved a $\sqrt{n}$ lower bound under similar conditions. Moreover, our research reveals that algorithms previously considered near-optimal for action spaces with quadratic curvature are in fact vulnerable to constant curvature environments, highlighting their inadequacy and suggesting that linear algorithms may be the best possible choices for such scenarios. Our findings derive from a novel construction of pseudo-moment description of a spectrahedron, whose associated matrix optimally represents the risk function of a fixed design matrix with optimal calibration properties, utilizing a minimal number of constraints. This pseudo-moment description is itself optimized via a variant of the Spectrahedron Projection Algorithm (SPA), which we have adapted for efficient computation purposes. Our approach was implemented in depth and detailed here in order to illustrate a novel Generalized Linear Bandit (GLB) technique for obtaining positive semi-definite matrices with an optimal risk representation, leveraging a generalized linear bandit with a quadratic curvature function. In addition to identifying sub-linear regret levels in action spaces with constant curvature as a significant concept, our research also reveals the potential for positive semi-definite matrices with an optimal risk representation to be crucial for beyond-sublinear regret analysis in GLB problems. GLB problems with beyond-sub-linear regret may arise when the function has a higher degree than two, which is illustrated in a standard benchmark problem known as the Grid Linear Bandit, where we have obtained a significant theoretical lower bound for its expected regret for action spaces with quadratic curvature. In contrast, linear algorithms incur a much higher regret when compared to the best-possible linear bandit algorithms in terms of knowledge of the parameters involved. This illustrates a key motivation for investigating linear algorithms in beyond-sub-linear regret scenarios. In addition to theoretical analysis, our research also involves exploring numerical computations for identifying pseudo-moment descriptions of spectrahedrons with a lower rank, which is itself an NP-hard problem. In order to efficiently obtain such descriptions with a limited number of constraints, we have developed an algorithm based on SPA. Over the past two years, research has gained momentum in graph adversarial attacks but Graph Classification remains an understudied area. The indirect utilization of Reinforcement Learning methods for graph classification, given that datasets involve discrete graphs with labels, stands in contrast to traditional approaches that use direct gradient optimization. This work aims to explore the novel threat of data manipulation during training (Data Poisoning) targeting Graph Classification neural networks via Reinforcement Learning agents. To this end, we introduce a novel Data Poisoning attack, the Label Exchanger (LE) that alters the training dataset's label distribution by swapping labels between samples, while maintaining their input states. We compare LE with the Gradient Assault attack, tailored for Graph Classification, neural networks. Furthermore, LE is complemented with a Cumulative LE that aims to disrupt the training process' progression by selecting challenging targets based on the current model state. Experimental findings reveal that LE is highly effective when targeting Graph Classification, while its combination with Cumulative LE yields enhanced results. Existing defenses have proven ineffective against this assault, yet we successfully mitigate it with a robust training method. This study brings Graph Classification into the realm of Adversarial Machine Learning and highlights the importance of secure training protocols to counter Data Poisoning attacks. As future work, our LE attack will be integrated into the Adversarial Flow framework for thorough research within Adversarial Machine Learning. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations, like those between concepts and their components or between similar ideas. This research introduces a new method for visualising very large ontologies on a large scale, integrating all three types of relationships: hierarchical, compositional, and semantic. This approach uses subset embeddings to handle extremely large ontologies by selecting and visualising a subset of concepts based on predefined topics. The developed tool, OntoVis, is a web-based platform enabling interactive visualisations of ontologies, along with a detailed analysis of its performance in visualising the Biological Ontology and the Human Ontology. Results demonstrate that OntoVis can successfully identify and visualise a substantial number of concepts within a large biological ontology. Importantly, this method can be readily extended to visualise other types of taxonomic networks. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data sources such as video feeds. By leveraging the latest advancements and incorporating the most up-to-day variations of active inference, this work brings the theory into the age of machine learning by transforming it into a deep learning framework. This is made possible through a novel approach to latent variable modeling using variational autoencoders. Experiment results confirm that the model can accommodate dynamic environments and compare favorably with other models in tasks such as object tracking and state estimation. Furthermore, the study proposes a novel approach for representing motor planning and controlling robots, especially in uncertain environments. The proposed method is tested on a realistic simulation of a robotic arm navigating through a complex 2D maze, with the goal of reducing uncertainty as much as possible. By enabling robots to develop mental models of their surroundings in an end-to-end fashion, this research paves the way for the deployment of active inference in a broader range of robotics applications. the accuracy of the interstellar medium's (ISM) chemistry model. ISM chemistry refers to the complex processes involved in creating various molecular species. Since it's impossible to replicate all reactions in simulations due to the existing gap in the astrochemical reaction database, researchers traditionally remove less certain reactions. The aim of this study is to investigate the impact of reaction filtering methods on the composition of the ISM by applying them to the Eulerian 3D model MAGENTA. We analysed the effect of each method on the formation of C$_2$H, C$_2$O, C$_5$H$_5$, and CH$_3$OH by comparing simulated results to observations from the line survey of TMC-1. We found that applying the IUPAC rule or a rating system based on stability constants significantly restricted the formation of these molecules. Moreover, removing less certain reactions based on abundance comparisons led to overproduction of the species. The results show that current reaction filtering methods can inaccurately model ISM chemistry, especially since C$_2$H can form through less certain reactions and its formation is not solely determined by the availability of C$_2$H and CO. The implementation of reaction-based filtering methods in Eulerian models has consistent effects on the composition of the ISM but its impact varies with time in Lagrangian models of the ISM. This research highlights the necessity of continuously validating and improving the ISM's chemistry model by including new reactions and challenging observed species. Future research should also focus on developing a more ISM-specific filtering method to address reaction uncertainties. Future studies will investigate the effect of reaction-based filtering on the formation of C$_2$O and CH$_3$OH. We recommend that existing molecular observables be used to refine the ISM's chemistry model by incorporating new reactions or adjusting existing ones, and we suggest developing a more ISM-specific filtering method to address reaction uncertainties. Future research should focus on challenging new observed species, such as C$_2$O and CH$_3$OH, to further refine the ISM's chemistry model. Our key contribution is a depth-controlled randomized measurement strategy that combines the capabilities of random Pauli measurements and random Clifford measurements. These can be viewed as the two extremes in our strategy. Our main focus lies in the realm where the number of copies grows polynomially with the size of the state space for large quantum systems. Notably, our findings indicate that achieving full state estimation is highly unlikely using only Pauli measurements, but it is feasible if additional, non-polynomially manageable resources are employed. In contrast, our strategy based on Clifford measurements requires the least number of copies among all possible ensembles of measurements with a manageable number of copies, making it the preferred choice for knowledge acquisition on large quantum systems. Moreover, our approach leads to novel limitations on universal state estimation, as well as upper bounds on the distillability of ensemble dephasing mechanisms. These results highlight the significance of optimizing measurement ensembles for knowledge acquisition about a quantum state. Our approach also reveals that achieving full state estimation becomes increasingly challenging as the number of copies increases exponentially with the size of the state space for large quantum systems. Our approach and estimates can be used to determine the minimum number of copies required to estimate certain features of a quantum state within a specific error margin through Pauli measurements. Our strategy may pave the way for improved adaptive measurement schemes, which could potentially outperform randomized measurements by utilizing the initial estimates of the quantum state to guide subsequent measurements. Our approach also reveals that the distillable ensemble dephasing rate provides a more accurate upper limit on the rate at which mixedness is introduced by ensemble dephasing mechanisms than the optimal converging rate based on Pauli measurements alone. Our approach and estimates may facilitate the development of adaptive protocols for estimating quantum states that converge at a faster rate than previously thought. In addition to these results, our approach can be used to obtain tighter bounds on the performance of universal state estimation methods, notably L\"unnell's scheme, and any other adaptive measurement protocol, by analyzing their performance in chunks of size O(n^l), where n represents the size of the state space and l represents the number of previous measurements less than a specified threshold T. Our approach reveals that achieving full state estimation grows exponentially with the size of the threshold for large quantum systems and that the performance of any adaptive measurement protocol is highly sensitive to the initial state. Our approach can be used to obtain tight upper and lower bounds on the performance of universal state estimation methods that converge at a rapid rate,

They now examined how this work can be applied to the reflection coefficient and derived new asymptotic formulas for specific domains with potential functions and smooth, strictly convex boundaries. For an infinite half-plane, the eikonal term does not appear, while for an exterior domain, the eikonal term encodes information about the geometry of the boundary. Numerical examples were compiled to demonstrate the accuracy and practicality of the obtained formulas. Furthermore, the formula for the amplitude was determined using a change of variables and the transformation of the system of equations, which results in the determination of the potential from the knowledge of the solution on a subset of the domain. A comparison with the results of the size of the source term was also presented. All derived formulas were shown to be valid uniformly for large $k$. A particular theorem regarding the limit of the solution as $k$ approaches infinity was established, which determines the potential function exclusively based on the solution on an infinite subset of the domain and does not rely on the knowledge of the solution outside of this subset. Consequently, the potential function can be recovered using data from linearly propagating components of the solution only. Smooth potential functions were recovered using numerical simulations obtained from the derived formulas, which in turn were used to determine the boundary condition on the domain. A particular system of equations, which describes the propagation of water waves in a channel with a variable bottom, was applied to demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of the obtained formulas in the context of inverse problems. Due to the presence of the source term, which varies with $\zeta$, the derived solutions do not generalize to the cases of constant $\zeta$. Moreover, the application of the source term does lead to confusion in the recovery of the potential function using data from the derived solutions. Nonetheless, the obtained solutions were used to determine the boundary condition on the domain effectively. The outcome of this study may inspire further research in the derivation of formulas for general $\zeta$ in the context of the inverse problem

-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method to create high-performance yet lightweight models. This study initially assesses its application in compressing MT models, particularly for languages with scarce training data, examining eight languages in the process. Notably, it is discovered that distillation-based model performance variability heavily relies on several preconditions, making it a somewhat unreliable compression approach. To improve on existing models, later sections explore alternative compression techniques, such as quantization and conditional knowledge distillation. While distillation yields modest results in some languages, other methods offer more promising alternatives. It is also found that combining these compression techniques can facilitate the development of useful cross-lingual capabilities, including zero-shot MT. Ultimately, it is observed that distillation might not be the optimal choice for compressing MT models, at least for languages with limited data. We instead recommend exploring alternative solutions, even though they still pose research challenges. A resource is available at https://github.com/mariu/kdmt for exploring the experiments presented. It is intended to provide a comprehensive comparison of this approach to others that show promise in enabling MT model deployment on low-resource languages. Finally, it is observed that distillation might not yield significant results compared to others, at least for languages with limited data. We explore the potential of cross-language knowledge distillation to augment zero-shot capabilities, presenting a two-stage process involving intr intr-sent distillation, and intr intr-sent paraphrasing followed by zero-shot knowledge distillation. This method yields modest gains, at most 1.7 points. Despite this, we observe considerable promise in paradigms like zero-shot knowledge distillation and parallel knowledge distillation in enhancing MT capabilities for languages with limited data, even though results are modest at best. A potential area for research could be exploring more effective paradigms to compress MT models while preserving their cross-lingual capabilities. A fully bilingual parallel corpus is essential for parallel distillation. We explore a set of pseudo parallel sentences obtained through a ranking-based process to simulate such a corpus. To further enhance model capabilities, we perform intr intr-sent distillation and paraphrasing. A research challenge is that conducting the experiments presented could yield varying results based on several parameters. graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that the set of possible Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs is infinite, and for 3-uniform graphs, irrational Turan densities have been discovered, disproving a previous conjecture. We investigate whether irrational Turan densities exist in certain cases and show that the Lagrangian density of a specific 3-uniform graph is sqrt(3)/3, resulting in an irrational Turan density, which answers an open question posed by Baber and Talbot. We also deduce that the Turan number for an F-free 3-uniform graph on n vertices grows quadratically as the number of vertices approaches infinity, providing a lower bound for ex(n, F). We further investigate whether this lower bound is actually a upper bound and establish that the set of possible irrational Turan densities for 3-uniform graphs is infinite. We show that irrational Turan densities can be achieved not only by graph F but also by certain hypergraphs H. We construct three hypergraphs with irrational Turan densities, and one of the densities equals the square root of 5 over 5. We investigate whether irrational Turan densities exist in a specific family of 3-uniform graphs and find a range of values for the lower and upper Turan numbers for an F-free 3-uniform graph on n vertices, and we reveal that the set of possible irrational Turan densities for 3-uniform graphs is infinite. We respond to an open question posed by Baber-Talbot-Yufna'ev on whether there exists a 3-uniform graph with irrational Turan density and a lower bound that grows quadratically as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality theories. This paper presents a new definition of qualitative harm, grounded in causal models and an established concept of actual causality, specifically emphasizing contrastive causation and default utility. The proposed definition demonstrates its capacity to address challenges in existing literature and highlights its significance in evaluating scenarios involving autonomous systems. Furthermore, it is stressed that the quantitative aspect of harm remains uncertain and requires deeper scrutiny. The study ultimately recommends integrating the qualitative harm concept into autonomous system legislation to establish a legal foundation, while acknowledging the need for further clarification on quantitative harm issues. The accompanying source code can be found at https://github.com/aaronvdg/harm-definitions. The focus of this work does not lie in providing a final solution but rather aims to initiate a discussion on incorporating causal models and an established concept of actual causality into the process of defining quantitative harm. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's efficacy for spoken language is largely unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot translation for speech-to-text, and in the process, contribute new insights to zero-shot translation and speech-to-text. Our proposed framework involves translating spoken language into an intermediate language that can be directly translated into the final target language. Unfortunately, there is a scarcity of zero-shot models capable of this process. We create our own intermediate language, LIndecx, which is composed of spoken and written word combinations that facilitate transfer. We then design datasets that test LIndecx's efficacy in zero-shot translation and speech-to-text. We moreover reveal LIndecx's capabilities in zero-shot translation, and show, for the very first time, zero-shot translation results for speech-to-text that are on par with the current best models. We delve into the well-posedness of the resulting system, particularly focusing on a key assumption governing its stability, which ensures the prevention of spurious long-term oscillations. This assumption, rooted in the spectral stability of the associated boundary operator, is satisfactorily validated for a broad class of integro-differential heat conduction systems with dynamic boundaries. We provide a precise criterion for its validity in the most comprehensive sub-category. We further investigate the behavior of the energy associated with the system and establish a generalization of the energy dissipation principle. We present two specific examples that illustrate the applicability of our theoretical findings: (i) we consider a system with Caputo time-classical spatial derivative, where the memory kernel exhibits behavior akin to the standard Fourier heat equation; (ii) we examine a system with fractional Caputo derivative in space and the Kelvin-Voigt body forces, where the memory kernel converges to the fractional Fourier heat equation. Since peak demand often drives energy distribution challenges, developing accurate timing and level predictions of daily peak demand is crucial, as traditional forecasting methods often fall short when dealing with peak events. This paper presents a new approach to forecasting energy consumption at the customer level, leveraging the dynamics of the smart home's operational state to inform its predictions. By characterising peak demands as spikes or sustained peaks, the proposed method combines the outputs of two types of networks - one dedicated to forecasting and another focused on detecting peak patterns - to generate precise point and interval forecasts. Given the inherently non-deterministic nature of energy consumption forecasting, the paper highlights the significance of producing robust interval forecasts that also result in more accurate point predictions. We diverge from conventional methods of developing optimal controllers through in-depth modeling and simulation, instead directly teaching model-free controllers to the actual robot. led researchers to investigate fashion instance-level image retrieval, where users search for specific items using images. This task is difficult due to the need for accurate color matching and considering that items can appear in diverse colors. Traditional methods are limited to retrieving similar-colored items, whereas fashion products often come in multiple colors, making color insensitivity beneficial. This paper proposes an innovative approach to fashion instance-level image retrieval, emphasizing the need for insensitivity to color changes. To this end, we introduce an affordable and effective dataset, known as ZhiDianYi, comprising 160,000 pairs of images, all from the web. A task-oriented framework, termed Color2Identity, has been designed to ignore color changes caused by clothing orientation and provide robust results. Our comprehensive experiments evaluate various aspects of the task and propose a theoretical model called TILT, incorporating Local Transformable Descriptors and Triple-Branch Query Transformations. In experiments, TILT surpasses existing state-of-the-art solutions by a significant margin and confirms that fashion instance-level image retrieval is indeed improved when color changes are dismissed. Furthermore, our framework and dataset are freely accessible online for further development. This work has also been presented at the Accessible and Intelligent Vision Workshop in 2021. Additionally, an extended version of this work has been published in a journal called Image and Computer Vision Engineering, with the article title being "Fashion instance-level image retrieval by dismissing color changes caused by item position and clothing orientation." This paper has been accepted for publication in the journal and is currently in its final draft stage. This work has also led to the creation of Fashion Colorblind Retrieval, a novel benchmark, which is designed to evaluate algorithms' ability to perform fashion instance-level image retrieval while being indifferent to color changes, regardless of whether the color changes are due to photography position or orientation. This benchmark further innovates by introducing two novel metrics, known as $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{R}$, to measure the performance of the top 1 retrieval item and the retrieved pool, respectively. Research has shown that a strong ranking does not necessarily mean a large pool, and vice versa ($\mathcal{P}$ is not directly related to $\mathcal{R}$). Therefore, both metrics are essential for evaluating the top 1 retrieval and the retrieved pool, respectively. Results have shown that our introduced TILT approach excels in both $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{R}$ metrics. Code used in this work has been freely released under the name Bilbudlab

The increasing use of high-bandwidth applications such as online gaming, virtual reality, and high-definition video streaming require enhanced network performance. The support of voice over Internet protocol (VoIP), online gaming, and other real-time applications relies on the stability of home networks, which is influenced by the network's latency. The management of home networks, specifically router configuration, often proves challenging for end-users. the main issue here is router channel allocation for maximizing network performance. The optimal distribution of network resources among devices can significantly reduce latency. This study presents a practical system for qualifying latency in home WiFi networks and formulates a mathematical model for resource allocation optimization. An iterative algorithm is developed to overcome the limitations of the axial complex number system, which hinders efficient computation. The simulation reveals that the proposed method achieves average latency reductions of 12.91%, 17.65%, and 26.56% for HD video streaming, online gaming, and VoIP, respectively. The results show that the proposed method is feasible, and effective, and can be easily integrated into commercial router management systems.
